N: Why does every layer need an activation function (a nonlinearity)?
To make the numbers smaller
Without it, any number of layers equals one linear map and can’t learn curved boundaries
To speed up computation
To save memory
Linear of linear is linear: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x. Only with a bend are many layers stronger than one. Tick “remove activation” in the lab and 6 neurons still draw a straight line.
What does backpropagation compute?
The next word
The best learning rate
The labels of the training data
Every parameter’s gradient: how much the loss changes if it changes a little
Backprop multiplies local derivatives back from the loss with the chain rule, getting every gradient in one pass; the parameters are actually changed by the “update” step that follows.
What is most likely to happen with too large a learning rate?
It overshoots the bottom, oscillating or even diverging
Training becomes more stable
The model gets fewer parameters
No effect at all
The gradient gives the direction; the step size is the learning rate. Steps wider than the valley overshoot and bounce back, and in bad cases climb ever higher (diverge).
Training loss keeps falling but validation loss starts rising. What is most sensible?
Train much longer
Raise the learning rate
Stop early (go back to the best-validation parameters) or add regularization / more data
Delete the validation set

This is overfitting: the model has started memorizing noise in the training data. The validation set exists to catch this moment; early stopping, L2, dropout and more data all reward simpler explanations.
Why did the Transformer replace the RNN?
It has fewer parameters
All positions compute in parallel and any two words connect in one step, so long-range information no longer fades
It needs no training
It doesn’t use matrix multiplication

An RNN must go word by word, and the first word’s information takes many steps to reach later ones; attention looks at all words at once, keeping GPUs busy and linking distant words directly. The cost is compute that grows with the square of the length.
Why do very deep networks with sigmoid suffer “vanishing gradients”?
Its slope is at most 0.25, and backprop multiplies by it at every layer, so after dozens of layers the gradient is almost 0
Sigmoid is too slow
Its output can be negative
It has no parameters
0.25¹⁰ ≈ one millionth. ReLU’s slope of 1 on the positive side, plus good initialization, normalization and residual connections, is what makes deep networks trainable.
T1: In “check the weather and add a reminder”, who actually calls the weather API?
The agent app (carrying out the instructions the model wrote)

The model only outputs a piece of text saying “I want to call get_weather”; the program does the executing. Separating “thinking” from “doing” lets the program validate parameters, control permissions and keep logs, and a model mistake doesn’t directly cause consequences.
Why split the system into app, model, training and compute layers?
Each layer does one job and can be replaced and improved separately
Because the model is too small
Layering lets the layers cooperate through clear interfaces: swap in a stronger model without rewriting the tools; add a new tool without retraining the model.
When you chat with an AI, are the model’s parameters changed by your conversation in real time?
Usually not: parameters are read-only in use; “remembering” relies on context and external memory

Training and use are two separate phases. Parameters are frozen in use so the same model can serve many people stably at once; things that need “remembering” go in the context or external storage. The “memory” features in AI products work the same way: your preferences and key past details are stored outside the model and retrieved into the context in later chats, without changing any parameters. That’s why you can view or delete those memories, and why they don’t affect anyone else using the same model.
T2: Why does an agent “loop” instead of answering in one go?
Looping costs more, so it’s better
Many tasks need a tool result before deciding the next step
The model can only output one character at a time
To make the user wait longer

“Create a reminder only if it rains” — step two depends on the result of step one. The loop lets the model decide each time based on the latest observation; a task with several steps takes several loops.
Why do “write actions” (sending email, creating reminders) usually need human confirmation?
They have real consequences and are hard to undo; confirmation catches misjudgements and prompt injection
A misread can be reread, but a wrongly sent email can’t be recalled. Handing the final gate to a person is the cheapest and most reliable safety measure.
What problem does RAG (retrieve first, then answer) mainly solve?
Lets the model use material it never saw in training, or that changes often, and cite sources

The knowledge in the parameters is a “snapshot” from training time, and it’s fuzzy on details. Putting relevant material into the context in real time lets the model answer from it, and makes checking easier.
T3: Why cut text into “subword” tokens rather than whole words or single bytes?
A whole-word vocabulary is too big and can’t handle new words, while byte sequences are too long; subwords are the compromise
Common words stay whole (short sequences), rare words are split (new words are no problem), and anything truly unknown falls back to bytes (never “unknown”).
What happens if you raise the “temperature”?
It always picks the top score; answers become more certain
Probabilities flatten out and rare words are picked more easily: more creative, but more error-prone
Temperature only changes “how to pick from the probability table”, not the model itself. Low is steady, high is lively; different tasks use different settings.
Why is “guess the next word” a good training exercise?
The answer is hidden in the original text: any text can generate exercises automatically, so data is almost unlimited
It yields huge numbers of exercises without human labelling; and to guess well, the model is forced to learn grammar, common sense and reasoning.
T4: What is the main purpose of a residual connection (adding the result back to the original vector)?
Gives signals and gradients a “shortcut”, so dozens of layers can still be trained

Each layer only needs to learn “add a few notes to the draft”, and gradients can travel along the shortcut all the way back to early layers instead of being multiplied away. Try switching off the residual in the “Build a Transformer block” lab.
It pulls the numbers back to a common scale so they don’t keep growing or shrinking; training is more stable
When dozens of layers are stacked, the scale of the numbers easily gets out of control. Normalizing at each layer means later computations always see inputs of “about the same size”.
How do attention and the FFN divide the work?
Attention exchanges information between words; the FFN processes each word separately
Once separated, both parts are simple: one only “moves” information, the other only “digests” it; alternating many layers of them can do complex things.
T4a: Why must a text-generating model “mask” later words?
In training the later words are the answer, so not masking is peeking; in use the later words don’t exist yet
The mask makes training conditions match use: every position can only guess from the preceding text. Switch off the mask in the attention playground and see how “it” peeks at later text.
Different heads can attend to different relations at once (the previous word, what a pronoun refers to…)
One head can only produce one weighted average, so several relations get blurred together. Multiple heads each look their own way and are concatenated at the end.
With large dimensions the dot products get large, softmax becomes too sharp and gradients shrink; dividing keeps values in a suitable range
Multiplying and summing d numbers makes the result’s spread grow with √d. Dividing by √d brings it back to a scale “independent of dimension”.
T4b: Why does the FFN first “expand” and then “shrink”?
A higher-dimensional space has more “switches” to store and combine more patterns
To make the vector longer and nicer

After expansion comes the activation function (filter switch); different “switches” light up for different inputs, like looking up entries in a big dictionary, and the result is compressed back to the original size.
Turns arbitrary scores into probabilities that add up to 1, keeping their order
Probabilities can be used both to draw samples for generation and, in training, to compare with the correct answer to compute the loss.
T5: Why does MoE “save compute but not memory”?
Each word passes through only a few experts, so less computation; but all experts must sit in GPU memory, on standby
The router sends only k experts to work each time, but the next word could go to any expert, so all of them must be in memory.
Why does the KV cache speed up generation?
The K and V of earlier words are already computed; each new word only needs its own computed
Trading memory for time. The cost is that the cache grows with “context length × concurrent users”, hence compression methods like GQA and cache quantization.
What is the main cost of quantizing from 16 bits to 4 bits?
Coarser ticks, larger errors; with too few bits quality drops noticeably
It must be retrained from scratch
Most numbers cluster near 0, so 8 or even 4 bits is usually enough; large outliers stretch the ticks, hence tricks like group-wise quantization.
T6: How do multimodal models let an LLM “understand” images?
Cut the image into patches and turn them into vectors (like a series of special tokens), connected to the LLM through a projector
Convert the image to a file name
The model reads the pixel file directly
As long as they become vectors of the same shape as text tokens, the attention and FFN that follow can be reused as they are.
Why do diffusion models denoise over many steps?
With heavy noise only a blurry outline can be guessed; denoising step by step gradually fills in details
One step is enough; many steps is just habit
Each step does only the easy-to-learn small task of “removing a bit of noise”. Set the steps to 1 in the diffusion playground to compare.
What is the training goal of CLIP-style contrastive learning?
Bring matching images and texts close in vector space, and push mismatched ones apart
The web has huge amounts of “image + caption” pairs, so no extra labelling is needed; once trained, images and texts land in the same “meaning space” and can retrieve each other.
T7: What happens if the learning rate is set too high?
Each step is too big, overshooting the valley and oscillating, or even diverging
The gradient only tells you “which way to go”, not “how far”. Max out the learning rate in the “Learning rate & overfitting” lab and see.
What does very low training error but high validation error indicate?
Overfitting: it memorized the noise in the training data too
That’s why you keep a validation set the model hasn’t seen. Remedies: reduce complexity, add regularization (weight decay), get more data, stop early.
What happens if the reward design has a loophole (eating small cookies repeatedly scores forever)?
The agent exploits it to farm points instead of achieving the real goal
The agent automatically understands your real intention
Reinforcement learning only maximizes the score you give it. This is called “reward hacking”, a problem to guard against when doing RL on LLMs too.
U: Which of these is not one of the four things that tell ways of using agents apart?
The four are: who starts it, where it runs, what it can touch, your role. Underneath it is always “LLM + tools + loop”; whose model it is does not change the kind of use.
A routine replies to customer emails every day. What is the safest setup?
Draft first; a person approves before sending
Turn off logs to save space
Give it full access to the whole mailbox
A sent email cannot be recalled; it is irreversible. In an unattended routine that step stays with a person.
If each step is 95% reliable, how likely are 20 steps in a row all correct? (illustrative)
0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.36. Small errors add up, so long tasks need checks along the way (tests, confirmations).
Ua: Of the four “work alongside it” ways, which can touch the least?
A chat assistant cannot reach your computer or accounts; at worst it says something wrong. The other three can edit files, run commands or operate screens.
Where should a command-line agent’s “fully automatic” level be used?
An isolated environment such as a container or VM
Fully automatic means no command asks you first; only acceptable in isolation, where a mistake costs little.
What does a “rules file” in the project do?
It is read into the context every time, so you never repeat yourself
A rules file is just text that is always put into the context; it changes no model parameters.
When a computer-use agent reads web pages, what must you guard against most?
Prompt injection hidden in the page text
Page text enters the context and may hide instructions like “ignore your previous instructions…”; so run it in isolation and confirm key actions.
Ub: What does a background / cloud agent usually hand back?
A branch or pull request (PR) for you to review
Changes made directly on the main line
Nothing
A new model
With a PR, the worst case is “do not merge”; a person takes the merge step.
A routine should be “idempotent”. What does that mean?
Each run gives a random result
It can only run once
Running twice on the same item has the effect of once
The more runs the better
So retries and catch-up runs never send or charge twice; a common way is to check “already handled?” first.
Which task fits a multi-agent team best?
Each step depends on the previous one
It splits into independent parts
A one-line answer
It needs your decisions all the time
Only independent parts can run in parallel with clean contexts; when parts depend on each other, coordination eats the benefit.
Which task is the worst fit for a background agent?
Adding tests to existing code
Fixing a known bug
Upgrading a dependency
A design whose goal is still unclear and is decided as you go
Unattended work must be clear and checkable; work that needs frequent decisions fits “work alongside it” better.
Uc: What problem does MCP mainly solve?
Every AI app had to integrate every tool separately
Models are not smart enough
Training is too slow
Slow internet
With one protocol each side implements it once and they connect: N × M becomes N + M.
In MCP, what role does the AI app you are using play?
Server
Host
Resource
Prompt template
The host (the AI app) opens one client per server; servers offer tools, resources and prompts.
Before it is used, how much context does a skill take?
Its full instructions and all scripts
The whole folder
Only its name and a one-line description
None, and the agent does not know it exists
Loaded on demand: only the name and description sit there so the agent knows it exists; the full text comes in when relevant.
What is the most direct problem with installing too many tools?
The model’s parameters change
The computer slows down
No effect at all
The manuals crowd the context and it picks wrong tools more often
Every tool’s description goes into the context; more of them crowd it, and similar tools get confused.
Ud: A good brief states four things. Which is not one of them?
Goal
Constraints
Praise for the model
Acceptance criteria
The four are goal, background, constraints and acceptance; pleasantries add no information.
Studies found that many models make worse use of which part of a long context?
The middle
The start
The end
All parts equally
A common tendency (the start and end get used more), varying by model; so do not bury key facts in the middle of a pile of material.
You switch to a completely different topic. What is best?
Keep asking in the same chat
Start a new chat, bringing a summary if needed
Paste all earlier chats in again
Make the question as long as possible
The old topic is noise for the new one and takes room; a new chat has a cleaner context.
The agent says “done”. What should you do?
Believe it
Ask it to say it again
Look at the evidence: test results, diffs, sources
Ask a different model
Models can be confidently wrong; judge “done” by evidence.
